newsitem.title: UK: LME copper stock tumble leaves market sceptical.
newsitem.headline: LME copper stock tumble leaves market sceptical.

text.p: The sharp drop in LME stocks Friday failed to provoke any sustained rally and simply prompted more questions about what was really happening to metal leaving the exchange's warehouses.
The fragile, brief copper contango was swept aside this week as LME cash to three months moved into a seemingly decisive backwardation of $18 to $20 per tonne.

"As long as the picture remains cloudy, then volatility will be the order of the day," said analyst Angus MacMillan of broker Billiton Metals. Friday's big LME stock drop of 18,450 tonnes to 202,500 tonnes, brought the total close to their lowest level since November 1995
Traders and analysts, however, point out that only U.S. demand is strong while Europe and Asia lag behind. Physical metal was not in such short supply to justify the big stock drawdowns, they said.
The market had predicted a drop of 17,000 to 20,000 tonnes, but views were divided over whether this reflected demand or a geographical redistribution of metal.

"Metal is just going out to a number of different destinations... We're talking North America, the Middle East, Europe and the Far East, and there are signs that there is more to go out," a senior copper trader said.
"It is not just a question of building stocks at plants, it is going out for consumption."
But Billiton's MacMillan believed much of the metal taken out of LME warehouses was material lent to the market earlier this year to exploit the strong backwardation and was now being taken back.
"The visible stocks no longer tell the full story. Stock movements are probably metal being shuffled around the system rather than reflecting real demand," MacMillan said.
Analyst Robin Bhar of Brandeis said Friday's LME stock fall was viewed cynically by the market which, under ordinary circumstances, would have rallied $50 to $60.

The senior copper trader agreed: "Around here, it is still too low...with this amount of stock and with what I've heard all this week talking to people who use the metal, it should be nearer $2,100 a tonne."

A speech during LME Metals Week by Herbert Black, Canada's most influential metals trader, brought the issue of Chinese copper stocks and Sumitomo's market position back into the forefront of traders' minds.
LME copper dipped slightly following Black's speech as the latest dose of post-Sumitomo jitters rippled through the market.

Bhar said it is believed that much of the metal leaving LME was not for consumption but appeared to be leaving Hamburg and going into bonded warehouses in China as a result of aribtrage deals with Shanghai.
As the metal is not being customs cleared, it could easily be exported, Bhar noted. "What's happening with the LME stocks may not be what it appears to be," he added.

Some traders privately suggested the strengthening backwardation was due to the sharp drawdown in stocks in recent weeks, and speculate that the reason behind the drawdown may be the desire by influential longs in the market such as the Chinese or even Sumitomo, to keep prices firm to make selling Such a strategy may prove difficult as MacMillan noted there was selling above the market and any rallies were likely to be shortlived.
The accident at the new El Abra mine in Chile helped firm up the market earlier in the week, traders said, but added that the effect was more psychological than real.
"But the market trades on perception," MacMillan said.
Cyprus-Amax which has a majority stake in El Abra and operates the mine, said the mine was operating and did not expect any copper contract commitments to be affected.
-- London Newsroom, 44 171 542-8075
